clips.send: 2007. Chang’e-1 orbits the Moon. The lunar programme is named after Chang’e (嫦娥 Cháng’é), the Moon goddess of Chinese legend. Its plan has three steps: orbit (绕), land (落), return (回). Chang’e-1 did step one and mapped the whole Moon.

clips.send: About 65,000 km (40,000 mi) beyond the Moon lies the Earth–Moon L2 point (a Lagrange point). There the pulls of Earth and Moon work together so a satellite can circle Earth in step with the Moon, using very little fuel. Queqiao (launched May 2018) doesn’t sit right on L2: it flies a big loop around it — a “halo orbit” — so the Moon never blocks its view of Earth.
